KEY MESSAGE 1...Active weather pattern through midweek with multiple 
rounds of showers and thunderstorms, including severe thunderstorm 
potential mainly late Wednesday through Wednesday night.

A northwest to southeast oriented complex frontal zone will remain 
in place across the Great Lakes through midweek, with an active 
pattern continuing. The greatest timeframe of concern will be late 
Wednesday afternoon through the first half of Wednesday night, when 
the severe weather and flash flooding potential peak.

Today, a mid level shortwave will continue to move southeast across 
northern and eastern NY through early to mid morning. Large scale 
ascent from the shortwave will combine with frontogenesis and 
moisture convergence along the frontal zone to support periods of 
rain across Central NY and the North Country, but this will taper 
off later this morning. Farther west, weaker forcing will only 
support a few scattered showers across Western NY and the Genesee 
Valley through early to mid morning. There may be a few embedded 
rumbles of thunder, but coverage of any thunderstorms will remain 
sparse through this morning.

This afternoon, subsidence and a bubble of drier mid level air 
behind the departing shortwave will keep much of the area dry. The 
combination of diurnal heating, warm advection, and the arrival of 
another shortwave late in the day may support a few more scattered 
showers and thunderstorms across Central NY and the North Country, 
especially across higher terrain. Farther west, a few isolated 
showers and thunderstorms may develop along the lake breeze 
convergence zone from the Niagara Frontier east across the Genesee 
Valley and western Finger Lakes, but otherwise expect dry weather to 
prevail in most areas.

Tonight, any spotty showers and thunderstorms will end in the 
evening with the loss of daytime heating. Dry weather will then 
prevail most of the night. A few showers and isolated thunderstorms 
may move into Western NY very late tonight or early Wednesday 
morning as the weakening remnants of upstream convection move into 
the area.

Wednesday through Wednesday night, a strong mid level trough will 
advance east across Ontario and Quebec, with height falls and DPVA 
spreading into the Great Lakes in the afternoon and evening. An EML 
will be captured and advected to near Lake Erie, with EML induced 
capping allowing a reservoir of strong instability to develop across 
the southern Great Lakes. Convective initiation will focus along the 
northern edge of the EML where rising parcels can more easily breach 
the EML induced cap, with this occuring upstream during the 
afternoon with the arrival of large scale ascent. Clusters of 
convection will move ESE across the eastern Great Lakes from late 
afternoon through the first half of Wednesday night.

Severe Weather Potential:

Today through tonight, the severe weather potential will remain low 
but non-zero across the area. A notable lack of forcing for ascent 
from synoptic scale or meso-alpha scale features combined with 
warm/dry mid levels will likely keep any coverage of deep moist 
convection sparse this afternoon and evening. Effective shear is 
also quite modest today, with 20-30 knots of flow through the mid 
levels. Strong surface based instability will develop this 
afternoon, so if any isolated convection does form there will be a 
risk of isolated strong wind gusts and hail, but this will be the 
exception rather than the rule.

Late Wednesday through Wednesday night continues to look much more 
interesting, with strong instability, strong shear, and sufficient 
forcing all potentially aligning in time and space. Strong 
instability and strong effective shear will potentially support all 
convective modes, including bowing segments and supercell 
structures. The strong shear is producing elongated hodographs in 
forecast soundings, although low level hodograph curvature is 
relatively modest in largely unidirectional flow. The primary hazard 
will be damaging wind gusts, with a lower secondary risk of isolated 
large hail. PWAT values approaching 2 inches will also support some 
flash flood potential if training occurs. An isolated tornado cannot 
be ruled out given the forecast shear profiles. Ultimately, the 
degree of severe potential will hinge in timing and placement of 
mesoscale features which cannot be reliably resolved in model 
guidance at this time range. Stay tuned.

Central NY.
